name: Computer Science Foundations
description: The foundational concepts of computational thinking: formal logic, set theory, and recursion — the bedrock upon which all CS is built.

observation.question: What computational patterns do you notice in the world around you?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can identify computational thinking in everyday situations

principle.question: What are the core abstractions that unify all of computer science?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can explain how logic, sets, and recursion form the foundation

application.question: How do these foundations apply to real software systems?
application.completionEvidence: Student can identify foundational concepts in software artifacts

integration.question: How do these foundations connect to each other and to other disciplines?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can map relationships between foundational concepts

creation.question: How can you combine these foundations to solve novel problems?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can integrate multiple foundational concepts in a solution

content.explanation: Computer science foundations encompass the core abstractions that make computation possible. Logic provides the language of valid reasoning. Set theory provides the mathematics of collections and relationships. Recursion provides the mechanism of self-referential decomposition.
examples: Logic gates implement propositional logic in hardware
Databases store and query sets of records
Compilers use recursion to parse nested syntax
analogies: Foundations are to CS what grammar is to language
visuals: Map showing how logic, sets, and recursion interconnect

practiceProblems.problemText: Identify at least one example of logic, sets, and recursion in a web browser.

memorized.evidence: Can name the three foundational areas
canDo: Identify logic, sets, recursion as foundations

comprehended.evidence: Can explain how each foundation contributes to CS
canDo: Describe the role of each foundation

applied.evidence: Can identify foundational concepts in real software
canDo: Locate logic, sets, recursion in code
cannotDo: Analyze foundational choices in system design

analyzed.evidence: Can decompose systems into foundational components

evaluated.evidence: Can assess when foundational approaches are appropriate

name: Algorithms
description: The study of systematic procedures for solving computational problems: algorithm design, analysis, and optimization.

observation.question: How do you approach solving a multi-step problem systematically?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can describe their problem-solving process

principle.question: What makes an algorithm correct, efficient, and elegant?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can explain correctness, complexity, and design principles

application.question: How do you choose the right algorithm for a given problem?
application.completionEvidence: Student can select and apply appropriate algorithms

integration.question: How do algorithms connect to mathematics, engineering, and biology?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can map algorithmic patterns across domains

creation.question: How can you design a novel algorithm for a new problem?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can design and analyze new algorithms

content.explanation: Algorithms are step-by-step procedures for solving problems. An algorithm is correct if it produces the right output for all valid inputs. It is efficient if it uses minimal time and space resources. Algorithm analysis uses Big-O notation to classify growth rates.
examples: Binary search: O(log n) — divide and conquer
Bubble sort: O(n²) — simple but slow
Dijkstra's algorithm: shortest path in weighted graphs
analogies: An algorithm is like a recipe — precise steps that produce a result

practiceProblems.problemText: Write pseudocode for binary search and prove it terminates.

misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Speed is the most visible performance metric
misconceptions.structuralReason: An O(n log n) algorithm may be slower than O(n) in practice due to constant factors, cache behavior, or implementation complexity. Correctness and maintainability matter as much as asymptotic complexity.

memorized.evidence: Can recall common algorithm categories and their uses
cannotDo: Analyze complexity or design new algorithms

comprehended.evidence: Can explain how algorithms work and why they're correct

applied.evidence: Can implement algorithms and solve standard problems
canDo: Implement binary search, sorting, graph traversal

analyzed.evidence: Can analyze algorithm complexity and compare approaches
cannotDo: Create novel algorithms for new problems

evaluated.evidence: Can judge algorithm quality and choose appropriate approaches

transformed.evidence: Algorithmic thinking is instinctive — sees computational structure everywhere

name: Data Structures
description: The study of organizing and storing data for efficient access and modification: arrays, trees, graphs, hash tables, and their trade-offs.

observation.question: How do you organize information in your daily life?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can describe how they organize data in familiar contexts

principle.question: What makes a data structure appropriate for a given task?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can explain access patterns, memory layout, and trade-offs

application.question: How do you choose the right data structure for a problem?
application.completionEvidence: Student can select and implement appropriate data structures

integration.question: How do data structures connect to algorithms, databases, and operating systems?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can map data structure concepts across domains

creation.question: How can you design a custom data structure for a novel problem?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can design and implement new data structures

content.explanation: Data structures are ways of organizing and storing data so that they can be accessed and modified efficiently. Each data structure has trade-offs: arrays offer O(1) access but O(n) insertion; linked lists offer O(1) insertion but O(n) access; hash tables offer O(1) average access but no ordering.
examples: Array: contiguous memory, O(1) index access
Binary tree: hierarchical, O(log n) search when balanced
Hash table: O(1) average lookup via key hashing
nonExamples: Unordered list with linear search (no structure)
analogies: Data structures are like filing systems — different systems for different access patterns
visuals: Comparison chart of common data structure operations

practiceProblems.problemText: When would you use an array vs. a linked list? Justify based on access patterns.

misconceptions.statement: Hash tables are always the best choice
misconceptions.structuralReason: Hash tables have O(n) worst case, no ordering, high memory overhead, and poor cache performance. For ordered access, range queries, or memory-constrained environments, trees or arrays may be superior.

memorized.evidence: Can recall common data structures and their basic properties
canDo: Name arrays, linked lists, trees, hash tables
cannotDo: Analyze trade-offs or implement complex structures

comprehended.evidence: Can explain how data structures work and their trade-offs

applied.evidence: Can implement data structures and solve standard problems
canDo: Implement stacks, queues, trees, hash tables

analyzed.evidence: Can analyze data structure performance and compare approaches

evaluated.evidence: Can judge which data structure is best for a given context

transformed.evidence: Data structure thinking is instinctive — sees organizational patterns everywhere

name: Algorithm Fundamentals
description: Core algorithm design paradigms: divide and conquer, greedy algorithms, dynamic programming, and backtracking.

observation.question: How do you break a large problem into smaller pieces?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can describe strategies for decomposing problems

principle.question: What are the fundamental paradigms for designing algorithms?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can explain divide-and-conquer, greedy, DP, and backtracking

application.question: How do you apply each paradigm to concrete problems?
application.completionEvidence: Student can implement solutions using each paradigm

integration.question: How do algorithm paradigms relate to each other and to mathematical proof techniques?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can map paradigm relationships across domains

creation.question: How do you recognize which paradigm fits a new problem?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can classify and solve novel problems using appropriate paradigms

isomorphisms.mappingDescription: Divide-and-conquer is recursive decomposition with a combination step
isomorphisms.limitations: DP adds memoization to avoid redundant work

content.explanation: Algorithm design paradigms are general strategies for constructing algorithms. Divide-and-conquer splits a problem into subproblems, solves them recursively, and combines results. Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step. Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems by storing solutions. Backtracking explores all possibilities and prunes dead ends.
examples: Merge sort: divide-and-conquer sorting
Dijkstra's: greedy shortest path
Fibonacci with memoization: dynamic programming
N-queens: backtracking with pruning
analogies: Each paradigm is a different lens for viewing the same problem
visuals: Decision tree showing paradigm selection criteria

practiceProblems.problemText: Classify merge sort, insertion sort, and quicksort by paradigm. Which is which?

misconceptions.statement: Dynamic programming is always better than greedy
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: DP considers all subproblems while greedy only looks ahead locally
misconceptions.structuralReason: Greedy algorithms are correct when the problem has optimal substructure and greedy choice property. When these properties hold, greedy is often faster and simpler. DP is needed only when greedy choices can lead to suboptimal solutions.

memorized.evidence: Can name the four paradigms and give one example of each

comprehended.evidence: Can explain how each paradigm works and when to use it

applied.evidence: Can implement solutions using each paradigm

analyzed.evidence: Can analyze paradigm trade-offs and classify novel problems

evaluated.evidence: Can judge which paradigm is optimal for a given context

transformed.evidence: Paradigmatic thinking is instinctive — sees algorithmic structure everywhere

name: Fundamental Data Structures
description: Core data structures: arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and hash tables — their implementation, operations, and trade-offs.

observation.question: How do different containers store and retrieve items differently?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can describe how different data structures store and access data

principle.question: What are the fundamental operations and trade-offs of each data structure?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can explain time/space complexity for each structure

application.question: How do you implement and use each data structure?
application.completionEvidence: Student can implement and apply each structure to solve problems

integration.question: How do data structures relate to algorithms, databases, and hardware?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can map data structure concepts across domains

creation.question: How can you combine data structures to solve complex problems?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can design solutions using appropriate data structure combinations

content.explanation: Fundamental data structures are the building blocks of efficient software. Arrays provide O(1) indexed access. Linked lists provide O(1) insertion/deletion. Stacks and queues provide LIFO/FIFO access. Trees provide O(log n) search when balanced. Hash tables provide O(1) average lookup.
examples: Array: int[] arr = new int[10]
Linked list: node.next = newNode
Stack: push/pop/peek in O(1)
Hash table: map.put(key, value)
nonExamples: Unsorted array with linear search (no indexing)
analogies: Data structures are like tools in a toolbox — each designed for a specific job
visuals: Memory layout diagrams for each structure

practiceProblems.problemText: Implement a stack using only arrays. What operations are O(1)?

misconceptions.statement: Arrays are always faster than linked lists
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Arrays have better cache locality and O(1) access
misconceptions.structuralReason: For frequent insertions/deletions at arbitrary positions, linked lists are O(1) vs arrays' O(n). For prepend operations, linked lists are superior. The choice depends on the access pattern, not an absolute speed ranking.

memorized.evidence: Can name fundamental data structures and their basic operations
canDo: List arrays, lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables

comprehended.evidence: Can explain how each structure works and its trade-offs

applied.evidence: Can implement each structure and use it to solve problems

analyzed.evidence: Can analyze performance characteristics and compare structures

evaluated.evidence: Can judge which structure is best for a given context

transformed.evidence: Data structure thinking is instinctive — sees organizational patterns everywhere

observation.question: What patterns of valid reasoning can you identify in everyday arguments?

principle.question: What are the formal rules that make an argument logically valid regardless of its content?

integration.question: Where does formal logic connect to other domains of reasoning?

creation.completionEvidence: Student can construct valid proofs using direct, contrapositive, and contradiction methods

isomorphisms.pattern: conditional branching based on truth values
isomorphisms.mappingDescription: IF-THEN logic maps to base-case checking in recursion

content.explanation: Formal logic provides a rigorous framework for reasoning. Propositional logic deals with statements that are true or false, combined using operators like AND, OR, NOT, and IMPLIES.
examples: IF it rains THEN the ground is wet (P → Q)
The ground is NOT wet AND it is NOT raining
It is raining OR it is cold
analogies: Logic gates in circuits mirror logical operators
SQL WHERE clauses are applied propositional logic

practiceProblems.problemText: Construct a truth table for (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P).

misconceptions.statement: IF P THEN Q means P causes Q
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: In everyday language, if-then often implies causation
misconceptions.structuralReason: Material conditional only constrains truth values, not causal relationships.

memorized.evidence: Can recall definitions of AND, OR, NOT, IMPLIES
cannotDo: Construct a truth table from scratch

comprehended.evidence: Can explain WHY each operator works the way it does

content.explanation: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct elements. Core operations include union, intersection, difference, and complement.
examples: The set of even numbers: {2, 4, 6, 8, ...}

description: The self-referential heart of computation: recursive definitions, divide-and-conquer, and the relationship between recursion and induction.

observation.question: Where do you see self-similar patterns repeating in nature or daily life?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can identify examples of recursive structure

principle.question: What are the minimal components that make a recursive definition well-founded?
principle.completionEvidence: Student can explain base case, recursive case, and termination

application.question: How do you decompose a problem into smaller instances of itself?
application.completionEvidence: Student can write recursive functions and trace their execution

integration.question: How does recursion connect to mathematical induction, trees, and self-reference?
integration.completionEvidence: Student can prove correctness via induction

creation.question: How can you design a novel recursive solution?
creation.completionEvidence: Student can design a divide-and-conquer algorithm

isomorphisms.mappingDescription: Recursive base cases parallel logical base truths
isomorphisms.limitations: Recursion adds execution order and stack depth

isomorphisms.pattern: combining smaller instances into a whole
isomorphisms.mappingDescription: Divide-and-conquer splits a set into subsets; union recombines results
isomorphisms.limitations: Sets are flat; recursion creates hierarchical structure

content.explanation: Recursion is a method where the solution depends on solutions to smaller instances of the same problem. A well-formed recursive function has a base case and a recursive case.
examples: Factorial: fact(0)=1, fact(n)=n*fact(n-1)
Fibonacci: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2)
Tree traversal: visit left, visit root, visit right
nonExamples: An infinite loop without a base case
analogies: A dictionary that defines words using other words
visuals: Call stack diagram showing nested calls unwinding

practiceProblems.problemText: Write a recursive function to compute the sum of a list.

misconceptions.statement: Recursion is always slower than iteration
misconceptions.structuralReason: Recursive algorithms can have better time complexity (e.g., merge sort O(n log n)). Tail-call optimization eliminates overhead.

misconceptions.statement: You need to understand the entire call stack to write recursion
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Tracing recursive calls is mentally demanding
misconceptions.structuralReason: The trust-the-protocol principle: if the recursive call works for smaller inputs and the base case is correct, the whole function is correct.

memorized.evidence: Can recall the definition of recursion and identify base/recursive cases
canDo: Name the components of a recursive function

comprehended.evidence: Can explain HOW recursion works and WHY it terminates
cannotDo: Design recursive solutions to novel problems

applied.evidence: Can write correct recursive functions for standard problems

analyzed.evidence: Can decompose complex problems into recursive sub-problems

evaluated.evidence: Can assess when recursion is the right tool

canDo: See recursive structure in non-CS domains
